text: Édouard Debat-Ponsan exhibited a painting called Truth Coming Out of the Well at the 1898 Salon, and it was later offered to Émile Zola. He was a Republican and a veteran of the War of 1870, and he took part in the struggle to clear Captain Alfred Dreyfus. A pupil of Cabanel, he painted portraits of wealthy citizens, scenes of ancient history and scenes of peasant life. A grant from the academy took him to Italy. Later a trip to Istanbul inspired The Massage at the Hamman, now in Toulouse. His son Jacques became an architect.

Alonzo Chappel painted people and events from the American Revolution and early nineteenth century American history. He was born in New York City and died in Middle Island, New York. His ancestors were French Huguenots. Many of his paintings appear in J. A. Spencer's History of the United States of America, and Drafting the Declaration of Independence is an engraving made in 1857. His oil painting Fate of Jane Wells shows the Cherry Valley Massacre of November 1778 and hangs in the Gilcrease Museum in Tulsa.

Adolph Treidler made illustrations, posters, commercial art and wartime propaganda posters. His magazine covers and advertisements ran in McClure's and Harper's. He made ads for the Pierce Arrow automobile and for the French Line. His advertising for the Bermuda Board of Trade in the 1930s helped to promote tourism in Bermuda. He was born in Westcliffe, Colorado. He studied at the California School of Design in San Francisco and later under Robert Henri in New York, and in the First World War his posters showed women working in munitions plants.

Adriaan Jozef Heymans lost his father, a trader in window glass, when he was only seven. His uncle, the mayor of Wechelderzande, helped to raise him, and in that small village near Antwerp he first learned to love nature. He entered the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp in 1853, but he always thought of himself as mostly self taught. Three years in Paris left him strongly influenced by the Barbizon School. Back home he painted outdoors with other artists, who together formed the Grey School. In 1869 he married and settled in Brussels.

Altichiero was much influenced by Giotto, certainly through the frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua. He may have trained in Florence. He worked in Verona and Padua, and his frescoes survive in Sant'Anastasia in Verona and in the basilica of Sant'Antonio and the Oratorio di San Giorgio in Padua. For a long time people doubted that he painted them alone, because of a supposed partnership with a certain Jacopo Avanzo. Study of the documents showed that Altichiero himself made the frescoes in both places. Around 1364 he painted frescoes at the della Scala palace in Verona.

Auguste Oleffe painted seascapes and fishermen at Nieuwpoort, where he spent time on the coast with the still life painter Louis Thevenet. After his studies he worked as a lithographer and draftsman. He visited Paris to improve his skills. In 1898 he and Thevenet founded an artistic society whose first members included Charles Dehoy, Willem Paerels and Ferdinand Schirren. It grew to fifty members and was disbanded later. In 1906 he settled in Auderghem, where he painted portraits of family and friends from the art world, and museums throughout Belgium bought many of them.

Art historian Bernard Berenson first identified the works of Bartolomeo di Giovanni, but he did not know the painter's real name, so he called him the Alunno di Domenico, meaning student of Domenico Ghirlandaio. The name came from the predella that the painter made for Ghirlandaio's Adoration of the Magi in the foundling hospital in Florence. Archival research later yielded his real name. He was active in Florence and also worked with Sandro Botticelli. He painted many narrative panels and altarpieces such as the Madonna and Child with Four Saints, now at Mount Holyoke College.

Charles Jervas gave painting lessons to the poet Alexander Pope at his house in London. He was born in Shinrone in Ireland and studied in London as an assistant to Sir Godfrey Kneller. After he sold small copies of the Raphael Cartoons to George Clarke of All Souls College, Oxford, Clarke and others helped pay for his years in Paris and Rome. In 1709 he returned to London, where he found success painting portraits of intellectuals such as Jonathan Swift and Pope. He succeeded Kneller as Principal Painter to King George I in 1723. He also translated Don Quixote.

A childhood injury left Charles Sims lame in one leg for life, and he thought it pushed his art toward playful subjects and swift moving bodies in sunlight. He was apprenticed in the drapery business at first, but at fourteen he was sent to Paris, where he learned French. Then he turned to art. The Royal Academy Schools expelled him in 1895. He went on to paint bacchanalian scenes, and his painting Childhood was bought by the French State and is now in the Musée d'Orsay. In 1920 he became Keeper of the Royal Academy Schools.

Christian Gullager painted portraits and theatre scenery in the late 18th century. He trained at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts, where he won a silver medal in 1780. He moved to Boston by 1786 and set up a drawing academy at his house on Tremont Hill in 1792. He also worked in Newburyport, New York and Philadelphia. One of his portrait subjects was President George Washington, and he designed scenery for Boston's Federal Street Theatre. He died in Philadelphia.

Christoph Schwartz worked as a court painter in Germany and was also known as Schwarz or Schovarts. Joachim von Sandrart says he was born in Ingolstadt and made many frescoes and oil paintings while in the service of Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria. According to the RKD he studied with Johann Melchior Bocksberger. The two of them painted frescoes together in Augsburg and Wasserburg am Inn. He died in 1592.

Cornelia Johanna Pabst, known as Corrie, studied at the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague, and Henk Bremmer was her teacher. She came from Woerden. In 1939 her work was part of the exhibition and sale Onze Kunst van Heden at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. Her pictures include still lifes, among them a Vanitas. She died in Laren in North Holland, and her work is in the Centraal Museum in Utrecht, the Kröller-Müller Museum and the Rijksmuseum. Laren held an exhibition of her work in 2022.

Émile Loubon painted wide landscapes of Provence with figures and animals in them. In 1829 François Marius Granet took him on a study trip to Rome, where he stayed for two years. In Paris he met young artists such as Thomas Couture, and in 1833 he won a medal at the Salon. Later he tried to teach drawing in more realistic ways and started the first salon for friends of the arts in Marseille, which drew Delacroix, Corot and Prosper Marilhat. He disliked the color blue. In his later years it turned gray or brown in most of his works.

As a child Ernst Stöhr could not decide between painting, poetry and music. His father was a violin maker, and his uncle was a music teacher and composer. He chose painting. He began at the University of Applied Arts in Vienna in 1877, but he disliked the stiff training and moved to the Academy of Fine Arts two years later. In 1897 he and seventeen other artists left the Künstlerhaus Wien and formed the Vienna Secession. He wrote often for its magazine Ver Sacrum, and the twelfth issue was entirely his work.

Count Franz Graf von Pocci wrote countless puppet plays and children's stories. He also painted and composed. In 1855 he and Josef Schmid founded the Munich Marionette Theatre. Pocci hired the premises, drew stage curtains and designs and wrote pieces for Schmid's hero Kasperl Larifari. The theatre credits him with inventing the Punch and Judy show, and with 45 original works for its library. Their partnership inspired other puppet theatres.

Friedrich Wasmann spent most of his life in a part of the Tyrol that is now in Italy. He was born in Hamburg and began an apprenticeship at seventeen with the painter Christoffer Suhr. Study at the academies in Dresden and Munich followed, and then two years in Merano. From 1832 to 1835 he lived in Rome, where Friedrich Overbeck, Joseph Anton Koch and other Nazarenes influenced him. He later converted to Catholicism. He married Emilie Krämer in 1846 and settled with her in Merano, where he painted portraits and religious works and wrote a popular autobiography.

Giuseppe Molteni had to leave the Brera Academy for money reasons, so he learned to restore old paintings in Bologna as a pupil of Giuseppe Guizzardi. Back in Milan he soon became one of the most sought after restorers of his day, and he advised the Louvre and the British Museum. He painted as well. In 1828 he started a kind of portrait that showed costumes and settings in careful detail, and it brought him into competition with Francesco Hayez. In 1837 he went to the court in Vienna to paint Emperor Ferdinand I.

Griffith Baily Coale is best known for establishing the Navy Combat Art Program. He grew up in Baltimore, where his father was a prominent member of society. From 1909 to 1911 he attended the Maryland Institute College of Art, and then he went to Paris and studied at the Académie Julian with William Laparra, focusing on murals. He came home to Baltimore in 1915 and worked as a freelance painter. In the last years of the First World War he worked as a camoufleur. He painted ships at the Port of Baltimore.

Heinrich Adam studied painting in Augsburg and Munich and won notice as a landscape painter and engraver. He was born in Nördlingen, and his brother was the painter Albrecht Adam. In 1811 he stayed with Albrecht at Lake Como and painted watercolours, and two years later he engraved six hunting pieces after his brother in Milan. Later he painted landscapes and town views that are very accurate. His oil painting of the Max-Josephs-Platz in Munich is surrounded by 14 smaller pictures of new buildings, all in one frame. He died in Munich in 1862.

After training as a jeweller and goldsmith, Henryk Grabiński decided on an artistic career and went to Vienna, where he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts for five years under the landscape painter Albert Zimmermann. One of his landscapes won first prize. He studied in Munich and then travelled to Paris and Italy. Back in Poland he divided his time between Kraków and Lwów and made sketches in Galicia, the Tatras and the Pienins. For four years he taught landscape painting at the Academy of Fine Arts in Kraków. A serious illness later left him unable to walk.

Isaac Claesz van Swanenburg painted and made glass paintings in Leiden and Gouda. He studied for six to eight years in Antwerp with Frans Floris and settled in Leiden in 1565 after his training. He sat on the Leiden city council from 1576. He became mayor five times. During the Siege of Leiden he fled to Hamburg for a year, but he was back by 1574. He kept a large and respected workshop for oil and glass painting, and his pupils included Jan van Goyen, Otto van Veen and his three sons.

James Green became known for his portraits in watercolour. He was the son of a builder and was born at Leytonstone in Essex. He was apprenticed to Thomas Martyn, who taught natural history painting, and then entered the Royal Academy Schools, where Sir Joshua Reynolds noticed him. In time he copied many of Reynolds's pictures. In 1792 he first exhibited at the Royal Academy, and many of his portraits were later engraved, among them those of Benjamin West and Sir Richard Birnie. He died at Bath.

Jens Birkholm painted poor people in times of distress, some of them in homeless shelters, and these became his most important works. He was a pacifist. To avoid military service he worked as a travelling companion for visitors to Switzerland and Germany. In Germany he met Social Democrats, and in 1892 he settled in Berlin. His only training was an apprenticeship with an obscure local artist, but he painted with his friends Johannes Larsen and Peter Hansen and absorbed the influence of Kristian Zahrtmann. In 1906 he returned to Berlin to visit the shelters again.

Johann Andreas Benjamin Nothnagel painted pictures of Jewish rabbis and leaders. He was a German Jewish painter. Many of his pictures were imaginary portraits of famous rabbis who had lived decades before his time. Copies and sketches of them were later taken for images of various rabbis, and sometimes one image served for two different people. They have been printed in Jewish history books, and in the past 100 years they have become part of Sukkah ornaments. The Israel Museum shows one picture that was recovered from Nazi plunder.

At the age of three Johann Georg Schwartze left Amsterdam with his family for Philadelphia, where his father began a paint and varnish factory. There Emanuel Leutze taught him. In 1838 he returned to Europe and spent six years at the Düsseldorf Academy under Von Schadow and Sohn. He also took private lessons from the landscape painter Lessing. He painted portraits and historical scenes. In 1846 he married Maria Elisabeth Therese Herrmann in Koblenz, and their children included the painter Thérèse Schwartze and the sculptor Georgine.

Joseph Stevens painted dogs more than anything else, from dog portraits to dog markets. He was born in Brussels. His early pictures showed sentimental scenes in a Romantic manner. Later he turned to a more realistic view of dogs living on the street or working for travelling entertainers, and the French realist painter Courbet admired him for it. He was a pioneer of Realism in Belgian art. He also painted horses and singeries, which are scenes of monkeys doing human things.

Jules Lion exhibited at the Paris Salon before he emigrated from Paris to the United States in 1837. In 1840 he opened a daguerreotype studio in New Orleans, one year after the process was invented. A notice in the New Orleans Bee announced an exhibition of his daguerreotypes, the first documented photography exhibition in Louisiana. He became one of the first in America to draw a lithograph directly from a daguerreotype. He also painted in pastel. His main focus was a series of lithographed portraits of prominent Louisianans.

Kuniteru studied under both Kunisada and Toyokuni I in Edo, now Tokyo. He belonged to the Utagawa school of ukiyo-e. He made prints on a wide variety of subjects, mostly book illustrations and single sheet prints, and many of them show the growing Western influence on Japan. He used several names. As Kunitsuna II he concentrated on caricatures and scenes from his travels, but after he took his master's name he added sumo wrestling and the modernization of Japan.

Louis Hector Leroux painted some thirty pictures of Vestal virgins over his whole career. He grew up in a family of modest means in Verdun and was first apprenticed to his father, a barber. Scholarships from the city later paid for his studies in Paris. He entered the Prix de Rome competition three years in a row. He came close. In 1857 his painting of the resurrection of Lazarus won the Premier Second Grand Prix, and in 1860 his master Picot and others arranged a commission for him to copy Titian's Sacred and Profane Love in Rome.

Michele Pace del Campidoglio painted still lifes of fruit and flowers. He was born in 1625, either in Rome or in Vitorchiano. People called him Di Campidoglio after an office he held in the Campidoglio, the Capitol in Rome. One picture by him hung in the collection of John Churchill, the first Duke of Marlborough, at Blenheim. Many others are in England. He died in Rome in 1669.

The son of a doctor, Nakabayashi Chikutō showed an interest in art very early. At fourteen he and his friend Yamamoto Baiitsu, who was only seven, met Kamiya Ten'yū, a wealthy merchant who collected art and calligraphy and helped them with their education. His first works were copies from Kamiya's collection. He was especially influenced by ink drawings of the Chinese Yuan dynasty and by the techniques of Ni Zan. At twenty he opened his own studio in a small temple. After Kamiya died, he and Baiitsu went to Kyoto.

Okada Saburōsuke painted landscapes and portraits, and his women have warm skin textures and delicate features. His parents served the Nabeshima clan. He first learned western style painting under Soyama Sachihiko, and in 1893 Kuroda Seiki and Kume Keiichiro, who had just come back from France, introduced him to the Barbizon school. In 1896 he became an assistant professor of Yōga art at the Tokyo school of fine arts. He helped found the White Horse Society, which is said to be named after their favorite sake. In 1912 he started the Hongo Institute for Western Painting.

Paul Leroy spent his childhood in Odessa, where his father had a business, and he lived there until he was 17. That gave him an interest in the East. In Paris he studied at the École des Beaux-Arts, where he met the Orientalist painter Georges Landelle, and the two stayed lifelong friends. In 1885 he visited Turkey and Egypt with Landelle and Landelle's father. He studied Arabic, so that he could use Arabic script in his paintings and lithographs. His Portrait de sa mère, a parody of Whistler's Portrait of the Painter's Mother, won the Prix du Salon in 1884.

Pellegrino Tibaldi grew up in Bologna. His father was a stonemason. His first documented painting, a Marriage of Saint Catherine, was probably made when he was 15. He went to Rome to study under Perin del Vaga, and after Perino died he led the large fresco work in the chambers and doorways of the Castel Sant'Angelo. In 1554 he decorated a chapel in Loreto with frescoes and stuccos, and Cardinal Giovanni Poggi soon called him back to Bologna. In 1561 he met Cardinal Carlo Borromeo, who employed him in Milan mostly as an architect on the cathedral.

Throughout his life Philippe-Auguste Jeanron held passionate republican views, and his genre pictures usually showed common people. He was born in the military camp at Boulogne, where his father was a shoemaker for the troops of the Emperor. As a young man he learned by copying The Wedding at Cana at the Louvre. In 1828 he and his friend Honoré Daumier shared fifty francs for a sign they made for a midwife. He opposed the July Monarchy. After the February Revolution of 1848 he became head of the National Museums and Director of the Louvre.

Teresa del Pò, also spelled del Po, painted and made prints in the late Baroque period. She was born in Rome. She was the daughter of Pietro del Pò, his second daughter with that name, since an earlier Teresa, baptised in Naples in 1646, must have died in infancy. She is said to have painted in oil and in miniature. She also etched a few plates in the style of her father, among them Susannah and the Elders after Carracci. She became a member of the Accademia di San Luca in Rome and died in Naples in 1716.

Yan Liben painted portraits of Chinese emperors from the Han dynasty to the Sui dynasty. His best known work, possibly the only genuine survival, is the Thirteen Emperors Scroll. In 643, under Emperor Taizong, he painted the Portraits at Lingyan Pavilion, which honored 24 major contributors to Taizong's reign, and he also painted 18 portraits of the scholars who served Taizong when he was Prince of Qin. Tang writers Zhu Jingxuan and Zhang Yanyuan admired his paintings. He was also an architect. From 669 to 673 he served as a chancellor under Emperor Gaozong.

Ida Josephine Burgess, born in Chicago, painted pictures and murals and made stained glass. She studied at Cooper Union and the Art Students League of New York, where her teachers included Walter Shirlaw and William Merritt Chase. She studied further in France and showed at the Paris Salon in 1885. She made the mural for the women's reception room of the Illinois State Building at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. Later she decorated the entrance hall and the reading room of Lunt Hall Library at Northwestern University. She also exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago.
